We explore the properties of a black hole within this $f(R,T)$ gravity model, specifically a Kerr-like rotating black hole, by deriving its metric tensor within the static limit. Additionally, we investigate the thermodynamic behavior of this black hole using the first law of thermodynamics and the Smarr formula, which allows us to calculate its thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, we examine the first law of thermodynamics for the black hole at the static limit, where the pressure vanishes. Finally, we discuss the stability of this black hole using the heat capacity.

Numerous astrophysical processes can be more efficiently simulated using
general relativity with a cylindrical coordinate system, given its natural
symmetry. This work presents a time-evolving, non-rotating, and axisymmetric
framework for general relativity in cylindrical coordinates. It is based on a
known harmonic decomposition method and has been enhanced to account for the
complexities of curved space. By using this approach, the evolution of the
spacetime is determined from a specific initial state, and the method has
been tested with a known solution. Additionally, the code's performance has been
assessed using a model of a stationary black hole, and the results show a
tolerance to certain discretization errors. This work has also explored the
influence of a rotating black hole on a surrounding fluid, and the results show
a good agreement with a known solution. This approach can be used to model a
wide range of astrophysical scenarios, such as the collapse of a star, the
evolution of a star, and the dynamics of a disk.

The $D^{(*)+}_{sJ}$ mesons are produced through the $J/\psi$ decay to $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$ and $D^{*0} K^+$, and researchers have studied the decay modes $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$ and $D^{*0} K^+$ to understand these mesons. By analyzing $5{\rm fb}^{-1}$ $pp$ collision data from the LHCb detector, researchers have observed the $D^{(*)+}_{sJ}$ mesons and found that they decay in the same ways as previously discovered $D_{sJ}$ mesons. This suggests that the $D^{(*)+}_{sJ}$ mesons are likely to be the same $D_{sJ}$ mesons with higher mass.

This research investigates continuous fractal functions generated by iterated function systems (IFS) based on fractal polynomials. It specifically explores a new type of polynomial that meets the open set condition, enabling the function to have a continuous inverse. For functions with a positive and increasing fractional dimension, we prove that their fractal counterparts can be accurately approximated using a specific set of fractal Gasket points, similar to the behavior of fractal polynomials on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket.

Traditional Visual Question Generation models generate questions based on a single image, whereas Guiding Visual Question Generation incorporates multiple images, combining their information dynamically through a guidance mechanism. This research proposes two variations of the Guiding Visual Question Generation model, incorporating a pointer network and a channel attention mechanism, to generate multi-word questions. The first model incorporates a pointer network to enable the production of multi-word questions. The second model introduces a channel attention mechanism to dynamically select informative image features for question generation. Both models incorporate a channel and spatial attention mechanism to select informative visual elements. The experiments conducted on the MultiImageQA dataset demonstrate that the proposed models outperform the existing Guiding Visual Question Generation model.

We have conducted a series of simulations of dwarf galaxies, examining how supernova feedback impacts the formation of dark matter cores. We discovered that the suppression of dark matter cores is highly dependent on how quickly energy is injected into the system. We found that if energy is released slowly, dark matter cores form, but if the release is rapid, a strong feedback effect occurs. We also observed that the threshold for this feedback effect changes based on the mass of the galaxy, with more massive galaxies requiring more rapid energy injection. We propose a relationship between feedback strength and galaxy mass, which can be used to predict the formation of dark matter cores in galaxies. We found that our models are consistent with recent observations and can be used to predict the formation of dark matter cores in galaxies. We also found that the feedback effect we observed is due to the rapid energy injection causing rapid gas outflows, which can be used to predict the formation of dark matter cores in galaxies.

We have developed a set of preprocessing methods for higher-order logic formulas. 
Unlike other approaches that only handle a limited number of variables, our techniques can be applied universally. They are based on two distinct types of simplification - formula transformation and variable simplification - which can be executed concurrently. In addition, we have formulated strategies for precomputing and utilizing the derived properties of formulas after simplification through a process called saturation. Our methods have been implemented within the higher-order logic solver SatSol. Through comprehensive testing, we have found that these preprocessing techniques can significantly enhance the performance of the solver, often resulting in substantial time and energy savings.

Zero-sum games have been extensively studied in various fields, including biology, game theory, and physics, with dynamics described by the $2\times 2$ system $x_{i} \rightarrow x_{i} \frac{x_{i}}{\sum_{j=x_{i},y_{i}}x_{i}+y_{i}}$. In this context, we have discovered that this equation generates an oscillating solution, and we have also established a relationship between the system's time period $T_{0}$ and the coefficients of the quadratic equation $z^{2}-T_{0}z+\frac{1}{2}(T_{0}-1}=0$. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the system's time period $T_{0}$ can be either real or complex, depending on the solution to the inequality $T_{0} \ge 1$ or not.

Random forest models have been widely used for their ability to effectively model complex data. However, until now, little was known about how they behave when trying to make predictions outside of their trained data set. Our research shows that, mathematically, a random forest model behaves in a predictable, normal distribution pattern when making predictions, as long as the number of predictions made is very large. This finding has led to the development of new statistical tools for testing models and computing the accuracy of predictions made by a random forest model. Our study also found that, surprisingly, a random forest model behaves consistently in a variety of different data sets, a finding that has led to the development of new statistical tests for understanding how these models work. Our research also provides new insights into how these models make predictions and how they account for the strength of evidence in different parts of a data set, a finding that has led to a deeper understanding of how random forest models work.

This research paper examines the influence of electric vehicle charging and discharging on grid voltage by employing a linear voltage drop analysis. We establish a theoretical framework that demonstrates how the integration of EV charging/discharging has a more pronounced impact on grid voltage than conventional load conditions. To mitigate voltage fluctuations caused by EV charging/discharging, we develop two strategies: the first involves shifting the charging/discharging schedule of EVs, and the second entails shifting the power demand of non-electric vehicle road transport. Both approaches can effectively alleviate voltage instability by counterbalancing positive and negative influences on grid voltage. We also assess the effectiveness of these methods using case studies based on real-world data from the North America grid.

We have conducted a comprehensive computational study of samarium orthoferrite, using density functional theory to analyze the structural properties of SmOF and its electronic behavior. Our research involved determining the optimal lattice parameters and examining the structural changes that occur as temperatures increase. We also investigated the magnetic properties of SmOF and compared them to other related compounds, including SmTiO3 and EuFeO3. Our analysis of magnetic moments and their distribution revealed that SmOF exhibits complex, non-centrosymmetric behavior. To determine the structural stability of SmOF, we performed lattice parameter optimization and examined the symmetry of its structure at the atomic level. Our research showed that SmOF exhibits orthorhombic symmetry in certain conditions, but is non-symmetric in others. Our analysis of the electronic properties of SmOF and its band structure led to the conclusion that SmOF exhibits a metallic state. Our research also showed that SmOF exhibits a metallic state. Our research also investigated the effect of temperature on the Sm magnetic moments and found that SmOF exhibits a large magnetic moment. In ecology, species functional diversity is a critical factor in determining a species' or ecosystem's viability and influence on their surroundings. However, developing a universal measure to quantify this concept has proven challenging, largely due to the diverse range of species with their unique characteristics and complex interactions. We propose a comprehensive approach to categorizing and quantifying functional diversity across various taxonomic groups, grounded in the analysis of trait networks. This method involves constructing a functional diversity network for a species or ecosystem based on their species-level network connections, which are weighted according to species similarity and network structure. We then utilize network analysis to extract a limited set of functional dimensions that encapsulate the network's essential characteristics. These dimensions are then evaluated using a range of metrics, which capture different aspects of functional diversity. We apply this approach to a selection of ecosystems, including a forest, mountain range, river, and wetland system, to illustrate its applicability and utility in understanding the functional roles of species within ecosystems.

This research introduces an innovative method for optimizing building ventilation control systems, where a previously unknown or unexploited control strategy is identified through the application of advanced black-box modeling and system identification techniques. By leveraging the data-driven approach, a model of the system is first developed, followed by the use of grey-box modeling to incorporate physical insights and enhance model precision. The resulting comprehensive model enables the identification of the underlying control strategy. Utilizing the identified model, a real-time optimizer is implemented to automatically regulate the ventilation system, achieving significant energy savings of up to 16.7% and improved indoor air quality through enhanced ventilation. The proposed methodology offers a data-driven and model-based framework for automating HVAC control systems, enabling the identification of optimal operating conditions for enhanced energy efficiency, comfort, and efficiency.

Our findings suggest it could be a high-end luminosity SN Ic. We noticed its light-curve peaks at a relatively slow rate, taking about 20 days to reach its brightest point. Furthermore, the SN exhibits a relatively slow decline, taking approximately 150 days to reach a specific brightness level. The temperature-dependent magnetic behavior of two-dimensional and three-dimensional magnets is being compared, with a prediction that their temperature-dependent hysteresis properties will significantly differ. This discovery has the potential to greatly impact the development of temperature-resistant magnetic memory devices, with a particular focus on anode-based phase-change memory. Furthermore, the research found that 2D magnets exhibit hysteresis at temperatures as low as 50 Kelvin, which is significantly lower than that of their 3D counterparts. This discovery is set to significantly improve our understanding of the temperature-resistant properties of 2D magnets.

We investigate the effect of word image associations on the learning of grammar rules from unlabeled texts by unsupervised second language acquisition models. To achieve this, we have developed a data augmentation technique based on word image associations that can be applied to any text. This technique can be used with any image-mapped dataset and enhances its utility for models that utilize visual information to learn grammar structures. Evaluations conducted on the Universal Dependencies corpus for 15 languages have shown that models utilizing the augmented data display performance comparable to or superior to that of previous state-of-the-art models across 13 languages. Notably, our approach demonstrates exceptional performance when learning grammatical structures in languages with complex grammar rules.

Attribution maps, which highlight pixels that led to a model's prediction, are a valuable tool for understanding image classification model decisions. Currently, attribution methods such as DeepLIFT rely on a complex optimization approach that requires substantial computational resources. To address this issue, we introduce a new method, Fast Reference-Free Normalized Gradients, which uses a localized version of the gradient method to calculate attribution maps more efficiently. Our fast method produces results comparable to existing reference-free techniques while using significantly less runtime and being more scalable.

A novel type of thin-shell wormhole, characterized by an absence of reflection, is formed through the collision of two black holes of equal mass. This new structure exhibits unique properties, including a magnetic field, rotation, and the ability to emit electromagnetic radiation, and exists in a state of equilibrium with its surroundings.

We have established a novel functional inequality that generalizes the established log-Sobolev inequality to encompass a wide range of multi-particle systems. This new inequality yields a corresponding family of entropic inequalities for Markov chains, which in turn facilitate the derivation of non-asymptotic, high-dimensional concentration inequalities for extended systems comprising $n$ particles. This enables the analysis of the statistical behavior of functionals in these systems, even when they operate on a large number of individual components.

Researchers have been studying trimer covers in square lattices for nearly a century, with recent combinatorial efforts focusing on such structures. We have developed an innovative approach to determine the weights of trimer covers in hexagonal and square lattices by employing a combination of random walk techniques and ratio growth analysis. This approach allows us to calculate the exact distribution of weights in hexagonal lattices and provide an analytical solution for square lattices. Furthermore, our method has enabled us to calculate the critical exponent in hexagonal lattices and precisely determined it to be 1.5.

The goal of Universal Domain Adaptation is to transform a source domain's classifier by adapting to two types of shifts: (i) changes between domains and (ii) changes between target subpopulations. This task is challenging due to the existence of skewed target populations, which are characterized by imbalanced distributions of relevant classes. Current methods are ineffective in addressing this issue, as they either rely on expensive target labels or use labels from a different domain. This paper proposes a novel method called Entropy-based Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for addressing skewed Target Label Shift. This method uses unlabeled target data to estimate the target label skewness and adjusts the source classifier through Exponential Moving Average. Our method outperforms existing baselines on multiple benchmark datasets and is validated through ablation studies.

This research introduces a 3D reconstruction method that builds upon existing knowledge of objects, enabling the creation of detailed 3D models from 2D images using only basic camera information. Our approach enables the initialisation of 3D object models, obtained from sources like CAD designs, product specifications, or databases, to guide the reconstruction process. The method then refines the 3D object geometry by combining prior knowledge with camera and image data in a probabilistic framework. The approach is flexible and adaptable to different applications, such as reconstructing entire objects from 2D images or refining partial 3D geometries. Our method is thoroughly tested on multiple datasets and outperforms existing 3D reconstruction techniques that rely on prior knowledge.

Constructing query graphs is a crucial step in resolving natural language questions, involving the creation of interconnected, weighted graph structures that are then evaluated to yield an answer. Recent advancements in query graph ranking methods utilizing neural networks have achieved impressive results. Nevertheless, these methods face three significant challenges when addressing complex natural language questions: (1) generating comprehensive, balanced query graphs with numerous interconnected nodes, (2) accurately infusing contextual understanding and word relationships into the graph, and (3) generating and ranking query graphs in real-time, free from any preconceptions. To address these issues, we propose a novel, multi-stage query graph generation approach, which involves a two-stage process consisting of a preliminary graph generation stage and a graph refinement stage. In the preliminary graph generation stage, we employ a novel, multi-hop attention mechanism to efficiently produce a balanced query graph in real-time, while in the graph refinement stage, we utilize a contextualized scoring function to assess the contextual relationships between adjacent nodes in the graph, thereby generating an enhanced, contextually grounded query graph. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets - WikiQA and TREC-10N-1307 - demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding state-of-the-art performance.

This paper examines the inherent characteristics of polynomial composites and their ability to satisfy fundamental algebraic principles. Additionally, it investigates how they can be utilized to establish both solvable and unsolvable equations.

Entity disambiguation is a complex natural language processing task that requires the ability to resolve multiple possible interpretations of ambiguous words, often aided by contextual information found in both structured knowledge graphs and unstructured source texts. Despite the challenges involved, research has shown that learning to solve this task with machine learning models can be a highly effective approach. In this paper, we introduce a novel neural network model that excels at entity disambiguation by combining the benefits of both knowledge-driven and data-driven methods. Our proposed model, known as Knowledge-Driven Multi-Homograph Disambiguation (KMH-D), utilizes a knowledge graph to establish connections between entities and leverages the similarities between similar words to infer the most likely interpretation. Our research involves training and testing the model on the well-known YAGO-Schema dataset and the larger Wikipedia-based dataset from the SemEval-2015-Task-12, with results demonstrating the model's superior performance.

This research examines one-loop oblique corrections to the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), specifically the $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters, derived under the assumption that soft terms break supersymmetry uniformly across all energy scales. A detailed analysis of soft scalar masses within the MSSM reveals that the impact of non-uniform boundary conditions for scalar and gaugino masses can significantly alter the $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters, often by an order of magnitude. These findings are illustrated using non-universal boundary conditions with various assumptions at the Grand Unified Theory (GUT) scale, demonstrating that the $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters' behavior is contingent upon the non-universal boundary conditions and gauge couplings.

We introduce an approach to generate novel views of a dynamic scene from a single video, employing a combination of neural implicit representation and scene-specific temporal information. Our method utilises a space-time and color-dependent latent function to represent the scene, which is learned using a temporal guidance loss and a frequency-dependent loss. This latent function is further enhanced by a temporal refinement module, allowing for novel view generation at test time via an efficient sampling-based method. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in efficiently and accurately rendering novel views of dynamic scenes from a single video.

This research paper investigates a broad class of linear rough differential equations with a variable damping component. This variable component, influenced by a process outside the equation's scope, exhibits both path-dependent and state-dependent behavior. Following a finite-time blowup, the solutions to these equations are considered up to a certain point in time. A specific theorem is established to analyze the solutions to these equations using change-of-measure techniques, and this result is then applied to study the long-term behavior of the solutions to these equations. Specifically, under certain conditions, we prove that the solutions to these equations converge to a stable equilibrium point.

We propose a novel model called the random grain model's long-range dependence counterpart, which is derived from the random grain model. The random grain model is defined as the superposition of n independent Poisson processes with varying intensities. By transforming the random grain model through a specific mapping, we obtain a novel model known as the random grain model's long-range dependence counterpart, which is characterized by a scaling parameter and exhibits long-range dependence. Notably, this long-range dependence parameter is directly related to the corresponding Poisson process intensity. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the covariance function of this long-range dependence model, which is consistent with the random grain model's short-range dependence counterpart.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) are emerging as a vital component in the sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, providing an efficient means of signal enhancement through passive reflection. RISs, however, pose significant design challenges due to the extensive parameter space involved, encompassing the phase shifts and array configurations of the reflectors. This paper presents an innovative approach to RIS design, leveraging a deep reinforcement learning framework to concurrently optimize the placement and phase shifting of RIS elements. This novel framework is adaptable to diverse RIS configurations and transmission scenarios, including MISO systems with multiple transmit antennas. The proposed method is showcased through numerical simulations demonstrating its efficacy in achieving superior performance, such as higher transmission power and better transmission quality, when compared to conventional RIS design methodologies.

This research focuses on the n-player stochastic game, which is governed by kinetic equations with multiple interaction scales. It incorporates a variety of interaction potentials that vary based on the number of players. Unlike previous approaches, we do not assume these interaction potentials converge to a common limit as player numbers increase. Instead, we prove the existence of a unique equilibrium for this complex dynamic system, building upon previous kinetic theory and large deviation theory. To achieve this, we first derive a multi-scale kinetic model using a specific mathematical framework, and then use the theory of pseudomonotone operators to establish the existence of a steady state solution. We subsequently apply LDP to obtain the kinetic model's limit interaction potential, and demonstrate its consistency with the original potentials through a key lemma.

A new method of quantization-aware training has been developed to efficiently integrate binary neural networks into high-resolution CNNs. This approach, similar to top-k and binary ensemble methods, uses binary weights and activations within quantization-aware training. However, our method differs from prior approaches in that it does not require separate training for binary neural networks. Instead, we utilize a weighted cross-entropy loss function to optimize both high-resolution and binary neural networks simultaneously. This approach leverages the computational resources of the high-resolution network while yielding comparable performance and accelerating training. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to a broader range of low-bit quantization, resulting in significant speedups - specifically, a 40 times acceleration for 4-bit and 60 times for 1-bit quantization while maintaining near original accuracy levels.

The ignition of a white dwarf star, which results in a Type Ia supernova, can occur due to one of two mechanisms: a sudden explosion triggered by helium ignition in a thermonuclear environment or a gradual expansion triggered ignition of explosive $^{56}$Ni. The latter mechanism is supported by a model in which the white dwarf is surrounded by a He-rich layer, which ignites and creates a wave of shock that disrupts the star's envelope, slowing down its rotation and allowing the white dwarf to lose mass. The resulting mass loss is so great that it completely destroys the star, releasing a massive amount of energy in the form of a Type Ia supernova. The model also predicts the presence of a significant amount of radioactive material, specifically $^{56}$Ni, which is responsible for the supernova's light curve, and is consistent with observations of Type Ia supernovae.

The online learning environment is characterized by sequential data samples and the ability to adjust parameters based on each new input. A key finding indicates that, to achieve optimal performance in the long run, online learning requires a combination of computational resources that grows in proportion to both the size of the data and the complexity of the learning algorithm. This is particularly relevant in the context of deep neural networks, which necessitate substantial computational resources. A strategy known as gradient compression has emerged as a potential solution to mitigate this requirement. A theoretical framework has been developed to demonstrate that gradient compression can be effective in reducing the computational costs of online learning using deep neural networks, without compromising on performance. This framework has been applied to show that online neural networks can achieve optimal results by utilizing computational resources that grow in proportion to both the size of the data and the complexity of the learning algorithm, even when faced with gradient compression. A novel gradient compression technique has been developed, which incorporates a combination of data compression and random noise. This approach has been shown to achieve optimal results by utilizing computational resources that grow in proportion to both the size of the data and the complexity of the learning algorithm. This is particularly relevant in the context of online learning using deep neural networks, which are commonly utilized in the natural language processing domain.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about severe economic and health crises, necessitating the development of effective strategies to contain the disease's spread. Governments and health authorities have implemented a range of measures, such as lockdowns, travel restrictions, and mass testing and vaccination campaigns, to mitigate the outbreak's impact. However, these efforts have been hindered by several issues, including the lack of transparency, inefficient resource allocation, and widespread vaccine disparities. To address these challenges, blockchain technology has emerged as a promising solution, offering a secure, decentralized, and transparent framework for the health sector. This article explores the potential of blockchain technology to address the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on the health sector. It highlights the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain-based solutions and presents a comprehensive review of various applications. The review also identifies future research directions and provides a detailed analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic's effects on the health sector and the benefits of using blockchain technology.

This paper examines the effectiveness of using sentence embeddings as a preprocessing method for text classification. We combine sentence embeddings with a transfer learning approach using a BERT model and apply it to a 7-class sentiment classification task. Our approach demonstrates superior performance on the dataset, outperforming the support vector machine baseline by a significant margin in the shallow network.

We investigate the diffusion of quantum particles on a $d$-dimensional hypercubic lattice, which exhibits a finite-temperature phase transition between a critical diffusion phase and an insulating phase, where particle-hole symmetry is broken. By employing a real-time Monte Carlo method, we determine key characteristics of the transition, such as the critical boundary separating the two phases, where the diffusion constant exhibits critical scaling. Additionally, we analyze the critical exponent and the correlation length, crucial indicators of the transition's nature. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the transition and the system's effective dimensionality.

We investigate the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and interfacial roughness on the dynamics of quantum Hall ferromagnets within a specific framework. By accounting for spin-orbit coupling and its effects, we have developed a method to linearize the Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation, allowing us to model the precession of the magnetic ground state. Our analysis reveals that the precession's attenuation is influenced by the roughness of the interface, while its frequency is determined by the spin-orbit interaction. By studying the precession, we can derive the spin-orbit coupling constant, a key parameter in understanding the system.

We explore the behavior of one-dimensional conformal field theories under periodic driving conditions. Two distinct phases emerge, characterized by the presence of well-defined local observables and by the existence of specific winding numbers. A theoretical framework allows us to determine the critical threshold at which the winding numbers become infinite, and our approach is validated through applications to both integrable and non-integrable models. Specifically, we examine a conformal field theory with a unique structure, given by the combination of two distinct theories. A notable example within this framework is provided by the driven version of the Ising model.

In this study, we introduce a novel multimodal generative model that integrates both sensor and imaging data to create a comprehensive image representation. By utilizing a single model to fuse multiple sources of data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the model in a range of tasks. Notably, our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple tasks, including camera localization from LiDAR data, by achieving a median error of 0.04 meters using just 10 images and LiDAR frames. We also show that our model can perform as well as models trained on twice the amount of data, underscoring the benefits of our method.

This paper introduces a new class of systems known as Graph Symmetric Systems, which encompasses various models such as linear positive systems, consensus systems, and linear quadratic systems. For Graph Symmetric Systems, optimality can be enhanced through a distributed optimal control approach, which involves the construction of a distributed compensator that adjusts the system trajectory. The main contribution of this study is the development of a new distributed optimal control strategy, which is based on a specific type of transformation and can be applied to several fundamental problems. The results demonstrate that the proposed strategy yields an optimal trajectory with minimal cost, while also enabling the system to converge to a target state. The validity of these findings is illustrated by applying the new strategy to consensus, optimal averaging, and linear quadratic optimal control systems.

This study presents a method to reduce the computational burden of a labeled random finite set filter, specifically a type of filter used for tracking targets, without significantly compromising estimation accuracy. The proposed approach involves setting a limit on the number of supported objects and adjusting the filter's parameters to exclude non-relevant data based on a specific rule. To optimize performance, the filter's mean-square error is estimated, enabling the determination of the optimal number of supported objects. The proposed method is applied to a target tracking scenario, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing computational requirements.

Linguistic databases, such as Universal Declaration of Human Rights Dialects (UDHRD), are valuable resources for linguistic research that classify language features across various languages.  However, UDHRD's limited coverage of languages, and the lack of a robust system for extracting relevant information from texts, pose significant challenges to researchers.  In this study, we explore the potential of using a system that automatically identifies and extracts language features from texts, and then utilizes this information to make predictions in support of linguistic research.  A novel neural network model, called a 'feature predictor,' is proposed that uses a combination of a word embedding and a transformer to make these predictions.  In our research, UDHRD served as a benchmark to evaluate the performance of the feature predictor, and we also tested its effectiveness on X-lingua, an open-source linguistic database.  Our results show that the feature predictor, trained on X-lingua, demonstrated a high level of accuracy in predicting language features in UDHRD, and in some cases, even surpassed the performance of the X-lingua training data. The primary objective of reinforcement learning involves maximizing the cumulative reward, which is typically achieved by optimizing policies based on historical data. However, this approach can result in suboptimal policies due to a mismatch between training and test environments. To mitigate this issue, off-policy evaluation provides a framework for evaluating the return of a pre-specified policy in an unseen environment. We propose a novel approach to off-policy evaluation through conditional generative adversarial networks. By utilizing this method to generate simulated trajectories, we can evaluate policies in real-world settings. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods by conducting experiments on four reinforcement learning benchmarks.

The fermentation process in the biopharmaceutical industry is a costly and time-consuming process, essential for the production of various bioproducts. Given the high stakes involved, it is crucial to minimize the risk of process failure by accurately identifying the likelihood of success. A recent study proposes a novel method for estimating the success probability of the fermentation process using a Bayesian approach combined with a Gaussian process model. The proposed method utilizes historical data from a biopharmaceutical manufacturing plant to train the model, which can then be applied to predict the success probability of the fermentation process under various conditions. The approach can be adapted to effectively utilize data from pilot experiments, offering a promising solution for mitigating model risk and ensuring the success of the fermentation process.

We have conducted a comprehensive study on the behavior of the large polaron in the quantum theory of electrodynamic physics, specifically under the condition of extremely strong coupling between the electron and the electromagnetic field. By using an advanced variational method and starting with a well-structured wave function, we have accurately determined the energy of the polaron for arbitrarily large systems. Our results show that the energy of the polaron can be broken down into two distinct components: a momentum-independent term and a term that varies linearly with momentum. Our wave function-based model precisely captures both of these terms. Notably, the mass of the polaron, which is a measure of its effective inertial mass, approaches a value of 2m (the electron mass) as the interaction strength increases. Our findings are in line with the mass enhancement observed in the mass renormalization of an electron in a vacuum, and we have also explored the implications of this phenomenon for the behavior of the polaron in the quantum field theory context.

We investigate the properties of the electric field in a quantum state characterized by a strong magnetic field. Our analysis focuses on the temporal behavior of the electric field's correlation functions and the lifetime of its operator. Our results demonstrate that in extremely strong magnetic fields, the electric field's behavior is significantly impacted, resulting in an effectively static behavior, whereas the magnetic field is responsible for the system's finite lifetime. Utilizing the concept of generalized coherent states, we are able to derive exact expressions for the correlation functions and identify the system's asymptotic behavior. Our findings are further supported by a study using the Peierls method, which confirms the system's asymptotic behavior.

Our research demonstrates the presence of complementarity within quantum systems by leveraging the extension of a fundamental theorem in Banach spaces, which has far-reaching applications in linear operators and has been adapted from [K. Madler and E. Krause, Banach Spaces, 3rd ed., Springer, 2020, p. 105]. By employing this theorem, we derive a linear operator that exhibits complementarity, leading to a significant finding. We then develop a novel method for creating entangled states and investigate the complementarity of orthogonal states. Our investigation into complementarity also reveals its presence in certain types of unitary operators, particularly those that are not necessarily irreducible.

We generate an infinite number of codes that represent periodic arrangements, consisting of alternating non-expanding lines with orientations either the same or opposite. These codes are derived from previously established examples in codes that represent periodic arrangements, where every line has the same orientation.

The Borsuk conjecture posits that any bounded, convex shape can be divided into $d+1$ sets of equal diameter in $d$-dimensional space. Building upon this, the definition of Borsuk number in a bounded metric space is established as the minimum number of partitions needed to divide it into sets of equal diameter. The main objective of this research is to establish a maximum Borsuk number for any given bounded metric space by finding a convex shape within that space with the highest possible Borsuk number. This study demonstrates that for any bounded metric space, the Borsuk number is at most $D(V)+1$, where $D(V)$ is determined by a specific combinatorial problem related to the vertices of a polytope that represents the space. This result implies that the Borsuk number for any bounded metric space is bounded by a function that depends on the topological properties of a convex shape within that space.

We propose an approximation for the resolvent of a fourth-order operator, 
confined to a finite domain, when a small parameter is present in the boundary 
conditions. This framework can be applied to high-order problems, and we validate 
it through the analysis of a fourth-order plate equation, which is stochastically 
driven. We derive an explicit approximation for the solution of the resulting 
random equation and demonstrate how the approximation's accuracy improves as 
the size of the domain increases, yielding a sharp upper bound for the error 
measure.

Developing virtual assistants in low-resource languages is complicated due to the lack of data and expertise available. To address this issue, we introduce a multilingual training method that utilizes data from languages with abundant resources. This approach is showcased in a benchmark experiment for task-oriented dialogue systems, comparing monolingual and multilingual training techniques. Specifically, we conduct a detailed analysis of a Spanish dialogue system, releasing publicly for the first time a comprehensive Spanish dataset. This research also involves a detailed annotation process, highlighting the differences between standard dialogue and task-oriented dialogue annotations. Ultimately, our study reveals that the proposed multilingual training method yields better results than its monolingual counterpart.
